title: How do you give a strong recommendation at the end of a case?
description: The last 60 seconds are what the interviewer remembers. Answer first, reasons with numbers, risks, next steps.
hook: Give a strong recommendation by starting with the answer in one sentence, then two or three reasons that each carry a number from the case, the main risk and how you would manage it, and the next steps. Take about 20 seconds to prepare and speak for about 60, as if to the client's CEO. Many good candidates lose marks here because they are tired and replay the case instead of answering the question.
body:
In this guide

  • Why the last minute matters
  • Answer first
  • The four parts: answer, reasons, risks, next steps
  • Prepare in 20 seconds
  • Check the answer against the target
  • Stress-test your biggest assumption
  • A worked example: PackRight
  • Common mistakes
  • Check yourself
  • Where to practise next

Why the last minute matters

The recommendation is the last thing the interviewer hears, and it is what they write up. It also tests the skill consultants use every week: telling a busy executive what to do, why, and what could go wrong, in about a minute. A case with good analysis and a muddled ending leaves a muddled impression.

Answer first

Open with the recommendation itself: "I recommend entering the US through a distributor." Not "So, first we looked at the market..." The interviewer has just watched the whole case and does not need a replay. Leading with the answer is the core of the pyramid principle, and it is how consultants write and speak to clients.

If the honest answer is conditional, say so in the first sentence: "I recommend buying RePlast, but not at the asking price." A clear conditional answer is still an answer. "It depends" on its own is not.

The four parts: answer, reasons, risks, next steps

PartWhat to sayLength
AnswerThe decision, in one sentence5 seconds
ReasonsTwo or three, each with a number from the case30 seconds
RisksThe main one, and how you would manage it10 seconds
Next stepsWhat to do first, plus branches you did not reach15 seconds

Reasons without numbers sound like opinions. "The market is growing" is weak; "the market grows 8% a year" is evidence. Use the figures you worked out during the case: a payback period, a profit gap, a share of the market.

Next steps are where you park any part of your structure you did not get to: "...and as a next step I'd also look at the cost side, which we didn't cover today." It shows you tracked the whole problem.

Prepare in 20 seconds

Ask for a moment: "May I take a moment to put this together?" Then look at the goal box at the top of your notes and write four words down the margin: answer, why, risk, next. Fill each with a few words and a number. Your mini-summaries from earlier in the case, if you made them, are your reasons ready-made. See how to drive the case for those.

Then look up and talk to the interviewer as if they were the CEO. If the interviewer frames it that way ("The CEO walks in. What do you tell her?"), answer in exactly the same shape.

Check the answer against the target

Before you speak, compare your answer with the goal. Suppose the client needs $5M of extra annual profit. Your analysis found two credible levers: $2M from procurement savings and $1.5M from reducing returns. That is $3.5M, so a $1.5M gap remains. Saying "the target is achievable" would be wrong.

A strong recommendation makes the gap visible:

"I recommend two moves that together add $3.5M: renegotiating procurement for $2M and cutting returns for $1.5M. That leaves $1.5M short of the $5M target, so as a next step I'd look for a third lever, starting with pricing, or discuss resetting the target."

Keep one-off costs separate from recurring benefits. A $1M one-off implementation cost does not cancel a $2M yearly saving.

Stress-test your biggest assumption

Ask yourself: if the interviewer challenges the assumption the whole answer rests on, can I defend it? Say an expansion depends on winning 5% of a $200M market, so $10M of revenue. Be ready to say what supports 5%, such as a channel, an advantage or pilot data, and what happens if the real figure is 2%, which is only $4M.

A recommendation should not pretend the uncertainty has gone. Give the best-supported decision now, name the risk that could overturn it and say how you would test it. That is far more useful than "the client should analyse this further" without making a choice.

A worked example: PackRight

In the PackRight case, a packaging maker is deciding whether to buy RePlast, a recycler, for an asking price of $180M. During the case you found:

  • Recycled plastic will be scarce from 2028, and PackRight legally needs 120,000 tonnes by 2030. RePlast produces 80,000 tonnes, two-thirds of that.
  • RePlast is worth $120M on its own (10 × $12M of EBITDA). Cost synergies add $50M and a "green premium" on revenue adds $60M, less $15M of integration cost: $215M in total.
  • Without the uncertain green premium, it is worth $120M + $50M − $15M = $155M, below the asking price.

Weak:

"So first we looked at the market, and we saw supply and demand cross in 2028. Then we looked at the synergies, and one colleague thought there was $24M of savings but that was double counting. Then we valued it..."

Strong:

"I recommend PackRight buys RePlast, but not at a flat $180M. Two reasons: recycled plastic becomes scarce from 2028, and RePlast covers two-thirds of what PackRight legally needs by 2030. With all synergies it's worth about $215M to us, but without the uncertain green premium only $155M. So I'd offer around $160M upfront plus an earn-out of up to $20M tied to signed premium contracts. The key risks are integration and food-grade quality, so next steps are technical due diligence and talks with three anchor customers."

That takes about a minute to say. It gives a decision, numbers behind it, a way to protect the client from the riskiest assumption and concrete next steps.

Common mistakes

  • Replaying the case. Start with the answer.
  • Reasons without numbers. Each reason needs a figure from the case.
  • Hedging. "It could go either way" is not a recommendation. Choose, then name the risk.
  • Ignoring the target. If your levers fall short, say by how much.
  • Generic risks. "Execution risk" says nothing. Name the specific thing that could go wrong.
  • Going long. Past about 90 seconds, you are summarising, not recommending.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. How should a recommendation begin?

  • With a summary of the case
  • With the recommendation itself
  • By thanking the interviewer
Show the answer

With the recommendation itself. Answer first. Reasons follow.

2. Where do unexplored parts of your structure belong?

  • Nowhere: don't mention them
  • In next steps
  • At the start of the recommendation
Show the answer

In next steps. Naming them shows you tracked the whole problem.

3. Try it now

You found that a bakery chain's target cities are growing 8% a year, a new shop pays back its investment in about two years, but opening in five cities at once would mean moving three of the chain's best managers. Give a 60-second recommendation out loud.

Show a strong answer

"I recommend expanding, but in two phases rather than all five cities at once. The markets grow 8% a year and a new shop pays back in about two years, so the opportunity is real. The main risk is management: moving three of our best managers could hurt the existing shops. So I'd start with two cities, hire and train managers in parallel, and open the other three once the first sites hit their numbers."

Where to practise next

Practise recommendations on their own: take any finished case from the casebook, read the findings and give the 60-second version out loud, timed. Work through the course lesson on recommendations, and read how to deliver a 60-second recommendation for more lines to practise.
